facts: Haidt opens chapter 1 with his first solo horse ride, in 1991 in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, North Carolina, with eight other riders and a park ranger.
On a steep hillside path the trail turned sharply to the left. Haidt froze and did nothing while his horse and the horse beside it turned by themselves.
That moment gave him the image of himself as a rider on the back of an elephant; he has used it for years. The rider can steer only while the elephant has no strong desire of its own.

Older images of the same split: Ovid's Medea torn between love for Jason and duty to her father; Buddha's mind as a wild elephant controlled by a trainer; Plato's charioteer holding the reins of two horses, one obedient and one unruly; Freud's ego, id and superego, which Haidt pictures as a driver struggling with a lustful horse while the driver's father lectures from the back seat.
Haidt lists four divisions of the mind: mind versus body, left versus right brain, new versus old brain, controlled versus automatic processing. The last one matches rider and elephant.
Split-brain research: in the 1960s surgeon Joe Bogen cut the corpus callosum in patients with severe epilepsy; Michael Gazzaniga then showed pictures to one hemisphere at a time.

In Gazzaniga's chicken-claw test a patient was shown a chicken claw to one hemisphere and a snow scene to the other; the left hand picked a shovel, and the speaking left hemisphere, which never saw the snow, explained that a shovel is needed to clean out the chicken shed.
Gazzaniga calls the left-hemisphere explainer the interpreter; Haidt identifies it with the rider: it invents reasons without knowing the real causes.

Antonio Damasio's patients with damage just above the eyes kept their reasoning and IQ but lost emotional responses; they struggled to make even simple decisions and their lives fell apart. Haidt concludes that reason depends on emotion.
The rider cannot overpower the elephant directly. Haidt's advice is indirect: change your surroundings so the tempting thing is not there, and coax or distract the elephant instead of fighting it.
Willpower alone tends to fail like a tired muscle, while automatic processes carry on effortlessly.
scene_details: a steep trail turning sharply left while the rider freezes
a chicken claw on one side and a snow scene on the other, and a shovel explained as for the chicken shed
a charioteer with two horses, a driver with his father lecturing from the back seat
a wild elephant held by a trainer
tension: The part that gives the orders is the small part, and it still invents a reason afterwards.
opening_idea: Vary by language: the frozen rider on the trail; the shovel and the chicken shed; Medea; Freud's driver and father in the back seat.

lessons.idea: The rider cannot overpower the elephant, so to change a habit arrange the surroundings so the right path is the easy one, instead of piling up reasons.
lessons.anchor: the horse and its neighbour turned by themselves while the rider froze

reflect_final: Which habit have you tried to change only by giving yourself reasons, and what one change to your surroundings would make the other path easier?

use_cases.situation: You keep skipping a morning run.
use_cases.move: Lay out the clothes the night before so the path is easier.

use_cases.situation: A team agrees on a new process and then ignores it.
use_cases.move: Ask what makes the old way easier and change that, rather than repeating the reasons.

use_cases.situation: A friend knows they should stop doing something and cannot.
use_cases.move: Ask what makes it easy for them in the moment and offer to help change that.

pocket_idea: The rider cannot force the elephant, so change what is in front of it.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Haidt pictures your reasoning as a small rider on a huge elephant, so more arguments to the rider rarely move it.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Haidt first rode a horse alone in 1991. On a steep trail that turned sharply left he froze, and the horse and its neighbour simply turned. He took it as an image of the mind: a small rider on a big elephant. Gazzaniga's split-brain patient even explained a shovel as being for the chicken shed. So change the surroundings, not only the argument.
